sections.title: 'Al Tifnu' Regarding Images and Books of Foreign Religions
sections.html:
It is a Torah commandment that a person not turn after idolatry (avoda zara), that is, that he not turn to take an interest in and think about its modes of worship, even out of curiosity and without any intention of worshipping it, lest through his interest in it he be drawn after it, or lest his faith and his attachment to God be weakened as a result, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:4): "Do not turn to the idols." Included in the prohibition is not to gaze at statues or pictures of idols (Shabbat 149a), and not to watch their rites, read their books or view other materials of theirs, such as those found on the internet. It follows that one who goes to gaze at idolatrous statues or rites, even if he does so out of mere curiosity, without any intention of checking whether it would be worthwhile for him to worship them, transgresses the prohibition of 'Al tifnu' ("Do not turn") (Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 2:2-3). And if he enjoys their beauty, he also transgresses the prohibition of deriving benefit from their adornments (above 10:8).

Included in the prohibition of 'Al tifnu' is that one may not keep in the house books of a foreign religion, and this includes books of religions that hold a belief in a supreme God combined with other entities (shituf). And although according to most poskim these religions are permitted to the descendants of Noah (above 5:8, 10), since for Israel they are idolatry, a Jew may not read their books or keep them in his home. It seems that books of Islam too should not be kept; even though Islam has no idolatrous corporealization of God, since converting to Islam is as severe as converting to idolatry, so that if a Jew is coerced to convert to Islam he must let himself be killed rather than convert (above 4:7), their law is like that of books of idolatry, as explained in the next halakha regarding heretical views.

In general, the law of turning to idolatry or to heretical views can be divided into three parts: 1) Turning to and taking an interest in idolatry or heretical views, even out of mere curiosity, is forbidden (as explained in this halakha and the next). 2) Turning to them and delving into them for the sake of understanding the Torah is permitted (below, halakha 3). 3) When one does not turn to them in order to delve into them and think about them, but merely takes an incidental interest as part of broadening one's knowledge of history and the like, it is permitted (below, halakha 5).1

sections.title: Lo Taturu ("Do Not Stray")
sections.html:
In addition to the prohibition of turning after idols, there is a mitzva that a person not turn his mind to thinking about and taking an interest in evil views that could cause him to uproot one of the fundamentals of the Torah, as it is stated (Bamidbar 15:39): "And you shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes, after which you go astray." The Sages expounded: "'After your heart' – this is heresy (minut)… 'and after your eyes' – this is licentiousness [sinful thoughts]… 'after which you go astray' – this is thoughts of idolatry" (Sifrei there; Berakhot 12b). Heretical thought includes taking an interest in and studying heretical ideas, whether in the direction of idolatry or in the direction of doubting faith in God, the special quality (segula) of Israel or the Torah of Israel. As the Rambam wrote (Sefer Ha-mitzvot, negative commandment 47): "That He warned us not to stray after our hearts to the point that we believe views that are the opposite of the views that the Torah has obligated us to hold."

The intention is not to prevent questions aimed at clarifying the truth, or thinking in the fields of philosophy; rather, a person's intellect has a personal limit and a universal human limit. The personal limit depends on the learner's personal level. The more advanced his stage of Torah study and intellectual development, the better he is able to grapple with views contrary to his faith and to answer them with responses that will strengthen his faith. But if he tries to study these views before reaching the stage at which he can grapple with them, there is a concern that they will harm his faith. Not only that, but even profound words of Torah are not suitable for one who has not yet become accustomed to delving into wisdom and studying the Talmud (Shas) and the poskim. And even then, he should take care to study them with great attentiveness and in light of a rabbi's guidance, so that he not err and understand them improperly and come to a corporealization tending toward idolatry, or to heretical thoughts (Mishna Ḥagiga 2:1).

The universal human limit stems from the fact that the human intellect is limited, and even if a person becomes very wise in Torah and wisdom, there are realms beyond the grasp of the human intellect, and if he tries to think about them he will ruin his intellect's ability to think properly, and will inevitably arrive at positions of idolatry or heresy. This is what the Sages warned in the Mishna (Ḥagiga 2:1): "Whoever contemplates four things, it would have been fitting for him not to have come into the world: what is above, what is below, what is before and what is after. And whoever has no regard for the honour of his Maker, it would have been fitting for him not to have come into the world."

These personal and general limitations are meant to give a person the possibility of growing wise in Torah and wisdom without falling into grave errors through occupying himself with matters beyond his grasp. So too the Rambam explained (Guide for the Perplexed 1:32) that just as a person who strains to look at things that he is unable to see, such as the sun, damages his eyesight until he cannot see even the things that he was able to see at first, so too one who tries to think about things that the human intellect is incapable of comprehending damages his ability to grasp what he is capable of understanding. Therefore the Torah warned not to stray after thoughts that could lead to heresy. But its intention is not "to close the gate of inquiry entirely and to keep the intellect from grasping what can be grasped, as the ignorant and the negligent think, who are glad to turn their deficiency and foolishness into perfection and wisdom, and the perfection and knowledge of others into inferiority and departure from the Torah; 'they make darkness into light and light into darkness.' Rather, the whole intention is to make known that the human intellect has a limit at which it stops."2

sections.title: Permitted for the Sake of Torah Study
sections.html:
The prohibition against thinking about and taking an interest in various religions or in the views of heretics (minim) and deniers applies when this is done out of curiosity; but for one who has already grown wise in Torah and wisdom and wishes to study them in order to deepen his understanding of the Torah, it is permitted, and even a mitzva, to study them. As it is stated (Devarim 18:9): "You shall not learn to do according to the abominations of those nations," and the Sages expounded (Sanhedrin 68a): "'To do' you may not learn, but you may learn in order to understand and to instruct." Moreover, only a sage who had studied the modes of worship of all the idols, and the ways of sorcery and magic, was permitted to be appointed as a judge in the court (beit din), for without studying them he would not be able to rule and judge in their laws (Sanhedrin 17a; Rambam, Hilkhot Sanhedrin 2:1). Even after the destruction of the Second Temple, when the courts no longer judged these laws, the Sages studied the ways of idolatry and sorcery in order to understand the depth of the Torah's guidance (Sanhedrin 68a; below 19:3). Thus the permission to study in order "to understand and to instruct" is not only for the sake of deciding halakha in court, but also in order to understand the reason the Torah forbade these things, and to teach this to students according to their understanding.

Just as it is a mitzva for Torah scholars to study in order to understand and to instruct in matters of idolatry and sorcery, so too it is permitted, and a mitzva, for one who has already grown wise in Torah and wisdom to study the views of heretics, such as heretical philosophical conceptions. For through familiarity with foreign religions and views one can better discern the uniqueness of God's Torah and of the faith of Israel. And those who delve deeply will thereby be able to understand the questions that trouble the people of the generation and the various answers that have been given to them, as well as the advantage of the Torah's guidance, which encompasses all the virtues in wondrous balance and, through the mitzvot, provides an elevating and rectifying response to all the challenges that a person faces. In addition, through studying the various religions and views, the sages will know how to answer the claims that adherents of the various religions, heretics and deniers make against the Torah of Israel, as the Sages said (Avot 2:14): "Be diligent in studying Torah, and know what to answer a heretic (apikoros)."3

sections.title: The Educational Question
sections.html:
Although the principles are seemingly clear, in practice there is uncertainty: when is the study of foreign religions and views liable to harm the faith of the one who studies them, so that studying them is forbidden because of 'Al tifnu' and 'Lo taturu'; when is there no concern that it will cause harm, so that there is no prohibition in studying them; and when will studying them enable him to understand the Torah better, or to know what to answer heretics and those who are wavering, so that studying them is included in the mitzva of Torah study?

This question depends both on the person and on the environment in which he lives. A person of deep understanding and broad knowledge can, through studying foreign religions and views, deepen his understanding of the Torah. By contrast, if his understanding is simple, studying foreign religions and views may confuse his mind, and he will derive no benefit from them. And if there is a concern that studying them will harm his faith, by taking an interest in them he will transgress the prohibitions of 'Al tifnu' and 'Lo taturu'.

Likewise, one whose faith is firm and whose soul is stable can grapple with foreign religions and views and thereby deepen his understanding of the Torah. But for one whose faith is shaky or whose soul is sensitive, an encounter with foreign religions and views can shake his soul and undermine his faith. Therefore, even if he is a Torah scholar of deep understanding, he should focus on studying Torah in halakha, aggada and musar. And just as it is not good for a person with a sensitive soul to deal with burying the dead, or to counsel those who have become entangled in severe problems of sexual immorality, so too it is not good for his soul to grapple with foreign religions and views; therefore he should engage with them only to the extent necessary for him to understand the Torah and to answer a heretic.

Beyond a person's level and character, the environment also influences him. Two main factors exert influence: first, the standing of the faith of Israel; second, the degree of exposure to foreign cultures. To elaborate on the first factor: one who is fortunate to live in an environment where the faith of Israel is held in great esteem need be less concerned about the harmful influence of foreign religions and views, and if he wishes to study them in order to grow wise in Torah, he may broaden his knowledge of them with greater freedom. But one who lives in an environment where the faith of Israel is debased, even when his faith is firm and his soul is stable, should be more inclined to put off engaging with foreign religions and views, lest he not find the inner strength to grapple with them. However, sometimes, precisely in difficult periods, the claims that adherents of foreign religions and views make against the Jews trouble many, and then the great rabbis must study their claims in order to equip the public with answers to the accusers and the heretics.

The second factor: throughout the generations, many Jews lived in a closed society that did not encounter foreign religions and views; consequently these did not challenge Torah learners, those who studied them derived almost no benefit from doing so, and there was also no need to study them in order to know how to answer their claims. Even when Jews lived alongside gentile neighbours who worshipped idols, those neighbours were often not educated, and consequently there was no concern that Jews would be persuaded by their claims. Therefore, the Jews dealt only with the laws of idolatry and not with its ideas. But when the Jewish community was exposed to foreign religions and views, it could not ignore them, and consequently it was necessary to study them in order to answer their claims and to understand the uniqueness and advantage of the faith of Israel. This was generally the case in communities located in capital cities and in centres of commerce and culture. It was the sages of these communities who wrote the important books that grappled with the various religions and views, such as Emunot Ve-de'ot by Rabbi Sa'adia Gaon, the Kuzari by Rabbi Yehuda Halevi and the Guide for the Perplexed by the Rambam.

On top of these principles, in all generations and places there were rabbis who tended to extend the permission to study various religions and views even to young students, in order to deepen their understanding of the Torah, and there were those who tended to limit it to great Torah scholars, in order to answer heretics. In recent generations, in the wake of secularization, this dispute has intensified. The leaders of the Ḥaredi public tend to protect Judaism through separation and distance from foreign views, and even from Jews who do not espouse this position. By contrast, the greatest of our rabbis hold that in the long term, in order to protect Judaism and increase its influence, one must grapple with modernity and its outlooks, and study foreign views in order to deepen one's understanding of the Torah and to know how to answer a heretic. This was the view of our master Rav Kook.4

sections.title: Studying History and Academic Study
sections.html:
Within the framework of studying history, it is permitted to read about various religions that influenced the course of history. For in this way one does not turn to the idols to take an interest in their religion, but rather turns to studying history, and in the course of this learns in general outline about the various religions. As long as the foreign religion is not described in an attractive manner, but only its historical story is described, it is permitted. This includes being permitted to look at pictures of statues in textbooks, and to watch videos that also depict the various rites incidentally. For in this way one does not turn to them or honour them, and there is no concern of being tempted after them; on the other hand, there is educational benefit in becoming familiar with the statues and rites that the Torah forbade.

Likewise, there is no prohibition of 'Al tifnu' or 'Lo taturu' for one who wishes, incidentally, to look up an encyclopedia entry dealing with a foreign religion or a heretical view in order to complete his understanding of various matters. This is so because he does so briefly and incidentally; because he does so for a general broadening of knowledge that can contribute to his Torah worldview; and because in an encyclopedia entry the foreign religion or heretical view is not presented in a manner liable to attract.

As for a student who is required to take courses on various religions: on the one hand, the courses are given in a manner that does not encourage joining a foreign religion; on the other hand, he is turning to take an interest in foreign religions. In practice, according to what was explained in the previous halakhot, when there is a concern that the study will harm his faith, he must refrain from it. The same applies to courses in philosophy: if they are liable to harm his faith, he must refrain from studying in them. And when the student has a great need to take these courses, in order to advance in his studies or because of his personal interest in them, he must then intensify his study of books about the faith of Israel and its blessed influence on the world, until it is clear to him that there is no concern that these courses will harm his faith.

There is no prohibition against reading fantasy books that imagine various magical powers, since the reader knows that it is mere imagination.

Within the framework of studying art, when it is necessary, it is permitted to look at works of art of idolatrous religions, since in doing so one turns not to the religion but to the art. Moreover, one is not looking at the statue itself but at a photograph of it.5

sections.title: Heretical and Idolatrous Books of Gentiles and of Missionaries
sections.html:
Although a Jew is forbidden to read books of idolatry, one should not damage books of idolatry that are intended for gentiles. This is the law even when they are books of outright idolatry, because Israel has no mitzva to destroy idolatry and its accessories that belong to a gentile (above 3:9, note 7). All the more so one should not damage books of religions that hold shituf, such as those of Christians and Hindus; since according to most poskim gentiles are not prohibited from idolatry involving shituf (above 5:8-10), gentiles are permitted to study them. And when they are elevated through them in ethics and good character traits, there is even a virtue in this for them (above 9:5).

But if the books were written or sent by missionaries in order to make Jews abandon their religion, they must be destroyed, so as not to leave any name or remembrance of their deeds. Even if the missionaries wrote a Torah scroll, it must be destroyed, so as not to leave any remembrance of the deeds of those who wish to make Israel abandon their religion. This is also brought in the Talmud (Shabbat 116a): "Rabbi Tarfon said: May I bury my sons (an expression of an oath) – if they (Torah scrolls written by heretics) come into my hands, I will burn them together with the Divine Names in them. For even if a person were pursuing someone to kill him, or a snake were running to bite him, he should enter a house of idolatry and not enter the houses of these, for these know [God] and deny [Him], whereas those do not know and deny." And although they contain holy Names, they must be destroyed. "Rabbi Yishmael said: It is an a fortiori inference: if, in order to make peace between a man and his wife, the Torah said, 'Let My Name, which was written in holiness, be erased in the water,' then these, who cast jealousy, enmity and rivalry between Israel and their Father in Heaven, all the more so. And about them David said (Tehilim 139:21-22): 'Do I not hate those who hate You, O Lord, and do I not contend with those who rise up against You? I hate them with utmost hatred; they have become my enemies.'"6

sections.title: Pictures and Statues Made for Decoration
sections.html:
It is permitted to look at statues and pictures that were made for decoration, even though the same statues and pictures are sometimes made for idolatry. Some are stringent and hold that if one is not accustomed to seeing these forms of idols, it is forbidden to look at them even if they were made for decoration. But if they are forms that one is constantly accustomed to seeing, such as forms of idols stamped on coins, it is permitted to look at them. And individuals who wished to sanctify themselves were scrupulous not to look even at these (Avoda Zara 50a).

In practice, the halakha follows the majority of poskim, that the prohibition against looking applies only to statues and pictures that are worshipped, but it is permitted to look at the same forms of idols when they were made for decoration. This is also the general custom (BHL). However, it is not fitting to decorate the home with pictures of idols, even ones made for decoration.7

As we learned (above 12:8), it is permitted to look at statues whose worship has ceased from the world, or at fragments of statues found in archaeological excavations. Nor do they involve the prohibition of 'Al tifnu', for since their worship has ceased, there is no concern that a person will be drawn after them.

sections.title: Recordings and Videos of Music and Worship
sections.html:
One should not listen to or watch recordings of the rites of foreign religions, because one who does so turns to the foreign religion and transgresses the prohibition of 'Al tifnu'. In addition, by listening to or watching them he nullifies the mitzva to destroy their name, as it is stated (Devarim 12:3): "And you shall destroy their name." And it is possible that by playing the recording he also transgresses the prohibition: "And the name of other gods you shall not mention; it shall not be heard from your mouth" (Shemot 23:13; below 14:1). But listening to or watching the recording does not involve the prohibition of deriving benefit, since the prohibition of benefit applies to seeing and hearing the rite itself, and not its recording.8

It is permitted to watch actors performing the rites of an idolatry that existed in the past and has ceased. For since it has ceased, it is not possible to turn to it and be drawn after it, nor is it possible to honour it, and consequently there is no longer a mitzva to destroy it.

There is no prohibition against watching a film that deals with secular matters and incidentally shows a religious ceremony, because the viewer wants to see the film and not to turn after a foreign religion. However, when the rite is presented in an attractive manner, to the point that there is a concern that watching it might harm the viewer's faith, he must refrain from watching it, because of the prohibition of 'Al tifnu' (as cited above, halakha 5).

Some hold that it is not fitting to attend a concert at which a musical work composed for a foreign religion is performed, even if it has no words with religious content (Igrot Moshe YD 2:56; 111). And some forbid listening to these works even in a recording (Aseh Lekha Rav 3:4; Benei Banim 3:35). But it seems halakhically that as long as the work is performed outside a religious framework, and without voicing sentences with religious content, there is no prohibition. For such listening involves no turning to a foreign religion, it does not accord honour to a foreign religion, and it does not cause the name of other gods to be mentioned. And as we will learn in the next halakha, some permit even taking these melodies for prayer; all the more so may one listen to them in a secular setting. And perhaps even those who are stringent not to use them in prayer would be lenient about listening to them in a secular setting. Therefore, it is permitted to listen to classical works by composers such as Bach when they are performed outside a religious framework and no words expressing a foreign religion are said in them.

However, one who wishes to attend a concert that includes singing must check that the content is not connected to a foreign religion. But verses of Tehilim that were set to music by Christians to be sung in church may be listened to within the framework of a concert unconnected to religious worship, as long as they contain no additions belonging to a foreign religion.

One who listens on an electronic device to songs or works without understanding the meaning of the words need not be concerned that they might belong to a foreign religion, for as long as he does not know this, his listening involves no turning to, or honouring of, a foreign religion.

sections.title: Using Gentile Melodies for Prayers
sections.html:
According to many, it is forbidden to use a melody that is customarily played in the worship of a foreign religion for prayer in the synagogue, for since it is a melody of a foreign religion, it is repugnant to use it for matters of holiness (Sefer Ḥasidim 238; see above 10:9). One should protest against a cantor (ḥazan) who does this, and if he continues to do so, he is not fit to be a ḥazan (Magen Avraham OḤ 53:31; MB 83). Many are also stringent not to use in prayer the melodies of licentious songs, because thinking about the negative content of the song will impair one's concentration (kavana) (Kaf Ha-ḥayim of Rav Palagi 13:6).

On the other hand, some permitted using melodies that Christians would sing in churches for the purposes of prayer in the synagogue, since in their view the melody itself was not tainted by being sung in church, and if it arouses kavana, it is good to bring it into the prayer (Rav Yisrael Ḥazan; Ta'alumot Lev; Yabi'a Omer vol. 6, OḤ 7). And some held that melodies of gentiles may be incorporated into prayer only if they also serve secular purposes, but if they are designated for religious worship it is forbidden to incorporate them into prayer (Responsa of the Baḥ, Ha-yeshanot, end of 127). In Arab lands, the cantors customarily took tunes from Arabic songs, even when it was known that their content was immodest, and the rabbis did not protest against them (Aseh Lekha Rav 3:5; Yabi'a Omer vol. 6, OḤ 7).

In practice, what emerges from the view of most poskim and from the custom of Israel is that cantors should not copy melodies from foreign religions; but if the melody has changed to the point that it sounds like a different melody, there is no prohibition. The same applies to melodies that were found to have originated in idolatry, but whose origin has by now been forgotten, so that they are perceived as ordinary melodies.

It is permitted to adopt tunes for prayer from secular songs whose content is positive. But one should not adopt tunes from secular songs that contain negative content of frivolity and lust, as long as there are people who know the song's negative content, both out of respect for the prayer and because of the distraction of the worshippers. And when their negative content is not known, it is permitted to adopt them.9

sections.title: Meetings with Clergy
sections.html:
It is permitted for rabbis and public figures to meet with Christian, Hindu or Muslim clergy, and when the aim is to increase understanding and respect between nations and people and to prevent hatred, there is even a virtue in it. So the great rabbis acted throughout the generations, and so did our master Rav Kook, who met respectfully with priests and heads of churches, and so did the Chief Rabbis in the Land of Israel. Some of the great rabbis even conversed at length with priests on matters of religion and ethics and formed bonds of friendship with them, such as Rabbi Moshe Ḥagiz, Rabbi Yehonatan Eybeschutz and Rabbi Yisrael Moshe Ḥazan.

This was also the path of rabbis of the Rabbinical Council of America (RCA), who participated in interfaith meetings and conferences with Catholic and Protestant Christian religious leaders. However, the great rabbis of the Ḥaredi circle expressed sharp opposition to this. In their words, those who participate in these meetings transgress the severe prohibition of drawing close to idolatry, and the prohibitions of 'mesit' and 'madi'aḥ' (enticing and leading astray). For they claim that the entire aim of the Christians is to cause Jews to change their religion and convert to Christianity, and after seeing that they did not succeed through coercion and murder, they switched to a method of missionizing through propaganda. And through the participation of rabbis in the meetings, Jews will be tempted to listen to them and change their religion (Igrot Moshe YD 3:43; 5:15). Apparently, in their view, the meetings that great rabbis held with priests in the past were for the purpose of intercession (shtadlanut), only to the extent necessary, and therefore they did not lend a hand to missionizing.

By contrast, the rabbis who were more involved in the modern world held that there is no concern that these meetings will encourage conversion to Christianity. On the contrary, fear of these meetings, like fear of scientific studies and of openness to the modern world, might distance young people further from Judaism and lead them to assimilation. Rav Yosef Dov Soloveitchik also supported this position. It goes without saying that these meetings are suitable only for one whose Jewish worldview is well formed, and for whom there is no concern that he will be influenced by foreign views. In practice, many years have since passed, and reality has proven that these meetings did not cause Jews to convert to Christianity.10

sections.title: Joint Prayers
sections.html:
In prayer, Israel turns to the Lord, the God of their fathers, in a deep and personal way; therefore it is fitting that prayer take place in a congregation of Israel alone, and in the house designated for it, the synagogue. And when a Jew must pray alone, it is fitting that he conduct his prayer quietly and modestly, as befits the deep and personal bond between Israel and God, which is likened to the bond between husband and wife. Similarly, the Sages said that one who displays his prayer in an open and exposed place is considered brazen (see Berakhot 34b; Peninei Halakha, Tefilla 3:8).

Therefore, ideally, gentiles should not enter the synagogue during prayer. In addition, the entry of gentiles who are not participating in the prayer may disturb the concentration of those praying in the synagogue (see SA OḤ 90:23). However, when there is a need, such as to accompany a sick person or to deal with the synagogue's electrical system, they may enter, as has been the practice for generations (Beit Avi 4:42).

When gentiles, out of respect and a desire to draw close to the Lord, God of Israel, ask to enter the synagogue or to see the Torah scrolls, it is desirable to accommodate them. Just as in the Temple they would accept an offering from a gentile even if he was an idolater, so too it is right to accommodate any gentile who wishes to draw close to the God of Israel. However, when gentiles wish to enter a synagogue and see the Torah scrolls out of mere curiosity, it is right to avoid this, for the synagogue is a place designated for the bond between Israel and God, and it is not fitting to expose it to strangers. But if this would cause unpleasantness, and all the more so if enmity might develop, one should not prevent them from entering the synagogue.11

When necessary, in order to increase peace and faith in God, it is permitted to hold joint prayers with members of different religions, and so have many rabbis who are public leaders done, among them the Chief Rabbis of Israel. However, care must be taken that the prayer be addressed to God alone, without mentioning any idol or person. Likewise, it is forbidden to enter a house of worship of a foreign religion for this purpose. However, since this matter is complex, and the balance between the different values must be maintained, in each and every place the responsibility for agreeing to a joint prayer is entrusted to the rabbis of the locality and the community, and it is they who must decide between the value of peace between the nations and the strengthening of faith in general, and the value of preserving the uniqueness of the faith of Israel and preventing assimilation.12
